articles.title: With AO3 down, fanfic readers are in survival mode
articles.summary: When the internet’s biggest fanfiction repository vanishes from reach, there’s one thing you can still count on: a network of fellow fans.
articles.body: When the internet’s biggest fanfiction repository vanishes from reach, there’s one thing you can still count on: a network of fellow fans. Just ask the massive community of Archive of Our Own readers, who in the past few days have gone from panic to ingenuity after their beloved fanfic haven went dark. AO3 is home to more than 18 million works, including many sexually explicit stories (affectionately referred to as “smut”), and writing inspired by popular IP, such as “Harry Potter,” “Twilight” and “Heated Rivalry.” But last week, the Organization for Transformative Works, the nonprofit behind AO3, announced the site would be down for two to four weeks, citing a “security incident.” The prospect of weeks without AO3 sent shock waves through a community devoted to the platform’s uncensored storytelling and meticulous tagging system. Some went as far as likening the outage to life in prehistoric times or descending into madness. But their desperation also gave way to solidarity, with readers sharing tips with each other on how they can still get their fan fiction fix. In the r/AO3 community on Reddit, moderators have set up megathreads for the purpose of helping members find and share copies of their favorite stories. Some AO3 writers are uploading new chapters of their fanfiction stories to their Tumblr blogs. Others are creating shared Google folders. “There are always debates, different opinions and occasional fights within and between fandoms. But during the outage, I have seen people from completely different fandoms and backgrounds helping one another and working toward shared solutions,” said Ashmita, a 23-year-old AO3 reader and fanfiction writer from India who built a web tool to make it easier for users to connect Google Drive folders and navigate the hundreds or thousands of files inside. “It has been a beautiful reminder of how much these communities care about each other,” Ashmita, who requested to be identified by first name only to preserve her online privacy, added. Another public Google Drive link to a “Fanfic Emergency Fund,” created by author Berklie Novak-Stolz, has already accrued a deluge of works across a wide range of fandoms and genres. “The horrors may persist, but so do we,” Novak-Stolz wrote in a letter to readers. “We’re all going to be okay thanks to the wonders of humanness and community and storytelling.” As of Sunday, the Organization for Transformative Works said there are no further updates regarding the outage. The organization encouraged users to review certain recommended safety practices as the outage persists, such as clicking links from trusted sources, being wary of scammers and creating unique passwords for every website. In a statement to NBC News, a spokesperson for the Organization for Transformative Works said it will share further updates on the “security incident” as soon as verified information becomes available. “AO3 and the OTW were founded by fans, for fans. That ethos remains at the heart of our mission today, and we love seeing how fans mobilize and support one another, both through and beyond AO3,” the spokesperson said. “As fan[s] ourselves, we deeply empathize with the frustration and despair of losing access to AO3—and we’re heartened by the creativity, humor, and sense of community reflected in the flood of memes.” AO3’s absence has prompted other fanfiction websites and adjacent platforms to seize on an opportunity to attract more users. “We’re here to support you during this difficult time,” a post from Wattpad on X read. “while our spouse ao3 is still resting drop your fav fanfics and authors to fill the void,” the X account for Tumblr wrote. The audio erotica platform Quinn also enticed readers by offering a discount code citing AO3’s blackout. But some die-hard readers said there’s nothing like AO3, a space they laud for being entirely community-funded and free of advertisements. “To me, AO3 feels heartfelt,” Ashmita said. “It is a huge platform, but it still has the feeling of a niche community built by people who care deeply about what they are creating and sharing.”

articles.title: David Bowie's Scottish links celebrated in new exhibition
articles.summary: Hundreds of items from Bowie's personal archive are set to go on display at the V&A in Dundee.
articles.body:
As musician Nile Rodgers once noted, David Bowie did not just make art - he was art.

So it is apt that his life and work should be celebrated in the V&A Dundee, within earshot of the first venue he played in Scotland under his new stage name.

David Bowie and the Buzz were not even the headline act that night at the Palais de Dans in 1966, but it was the start of a relationship with Scottish fans which continues today.

David Bowie: On Tour is the first exhibition to showcase items from the singer's archive, which was acquired by the V&A in London in 2023.

Many of the 100 items selected from the 90,000 housed in the David Bowie Centre, which was built to contain the sprawling archive, have never been seen in public.

Among them, his first instrument, a saxophone, which his father bought him for Christmas in 1961, the stopwatch he used when songwriting, his 1988 passport and an advance copy of The Velvet Underground's 1967 record I'm Waiting for the Man.

Listen to news from Tayside and Central on BBC Sounds

It also includes a letter of complaint from his London neighbours in December 1973, addressed to a "Mr Bowy".

The curt missive reads: "We would be very grateful if you would be considerate enough to have the music played much more softly and stop at a reasonable hour."

Leonie Bell, director of the V&A Dundee, said: "It offers something very special, the chance to encounter personal and intimate objects which reveal how David Bowie thought, worked and continually reinvented himself."

Bowie meticulously saved everything from the early portion of his career, charting his rise to one of the world's most enigmatic and influential musicians.

He later worked with professional curators to document and order it so he could use his own personal archive to rework projects he had previously abandoned.

Bowie also used it to fill in gaps where his personal items had been given away or lost.

The show also examines Bowie's many Scottish concerts and the impact they had on fans.

John Reilly was only 11 in May 1973, when the legendary Ziggy Stardust landed at the Caird Hall in Dundee.

Images of Bowie in a striking Kansai Yamamoto bodysuit take centre stage in the exhibition above a case of Polaroid photos and memorabilia from the show.

Despite gathering much of it, self-confessed super fan John, a former Dundee United footballer, did not join the 2,500 fans inside.

He went on to right that wrong by seeing Bowie live 49 times before his death in January 2016.

But the Dundee gig remains the one that got away.

"I thought it would be like a football match, and I'd just crawl in under the turnstiles behind my dad," John, now 64, recalled.

"I've got a couple of pals who were there and frequently remind me of what I missed out on but I like to think I made up for it after that."

John gave his children the middle names Bowie and Dalglish to represent his two great loves.

He said the chance to see Bowie's legacy return to his home city would be an emotional moment and a reminder of the "escape" his music provided.

"The girls in my class would save pictures from their Jackie magazines and I'd collect them in scrapbooks," he said.

"Then it was records and posters and tour programmes.

"I've made friends from all over the world and something like this brings the whole Bowie family together.

"Only this time, instead of travelling around to see him, I can get the bus into Dundee and the bus back home again and see it all on my own doorstep."

Among Bowie's most famous Scottish performances was a night at the Glasgow Apollo in June 1978.

In an interview for Reporting Scotland, Bowie told reporter Fidelma Cook that it was one of his favourite venues because of the "exceptionally excited audiences, intoxicated with the idea of a theatrical show".

But much of that theatricality was learned in Edinburgh a decade earlier from choreographer Lindsay Kemp.

A programme in the exhibition from January 1968 saw him appearing alongside Kemp in a performance of mime, music and dance called Pierrot in Turquoise, which had first been staged in Edinburgh.

Two years later, the show was filmed at Edinburgh's Gateway Theatre for Scottish Television as The Looking Glass Murders.

He also brought Ziggy Stardust to the capital, although fans had to wait until 23:30 for the gig to start as staff at the former Empire Theatre - now known as the Festival Theatre - emptied the bingo hall which provided its main source of income.

Much later, Bowie would draw on the imagery, dressing as the character of Harlequin in the video Ashes to Ashes.

By then, he was much better established and able to commission Muppets creator Jim Henson to create life sized dolls, rather than borrow dolls from the Museum of Childhood.

"He played in Scotland multiple times in his career," said curator Svetlana Panova.

"While researching the Dundee performances we were struck by how vividly they still live in the hearts and memories of local fans who have proudly held onto their keepsakes."

Svetlana added: "Their dedication has made it possible to tell the cherished story of 17 May 1973 as part of the legendary Ziggy Stardust tour."

articles.title: He reimagined his parents’ wedding portrait, with their roles reversed
articles.summary: For 17 years, the Taiwanese artist Liu Hsing-Yu has photographed his parents, swapping their gender roles in his images. It has transformed their relationship in ways he couldn’t have imagined.
articles.body: When Liu Hsing-Yu asked his parents to swap wedding outfits and be photographed among a sea of plastic roses, he didn’t realize he’d be embarking on a 17-year-long (and counting) body of work. In 2009, he was studying for his art degree and had recently come out to them as a gay man — both of which they struggled to understand. In fact, as he recalled from his home in Taiwan, they initially thought that the former had caused the latter. At the time, Taiwan was still a decade away from legalizing same-sex marriage. Liu had the idea to subvert his parents’ roles after finding his father’s wedding suit from 1984. Given their traditional beliefs around gender and families, he was surprised when his mother said yes. His father took more persuading, but he eventually agreed, too. The resulting portrait was one of the first images in Liu’s series “My Parents,” which he has exhibited numerous times over the years, including the latest presentation at the UK’s Bristol Photo Festival, which opened recently. He is also publishing a book of the photographs. In the reimagined wedding portrait, his mother appears in his father’s suit and his father wears a secondhand wedding dress. They pose on their family’s farmlands, where Liu’s grandfather once grew taros, rice and mangoes. It’s near Taiwan’s southern port city of Kaohsiung, where Liu was born. “The relationships between these objects and the place were important to me,” he explained. “The farmland and the truck are connected to work and physical labor. The wedding dress and suit carry ideas about marriage and how men and women are expected to behave. Putting them together in one image made these familiar things feel slightly out of place.” At the time, his father, a truck driver, was nearing retirement and anxious about the transition. His mother was planning to find new work to support the family. Through their poses, with his father resting and his mother assuming a more assertive role, Liu wanted to reflect their changing dynamic. He thought about how gender roles inform our everyday responsibilities: “Who should earn money, who should provide care and who is allowed to show vulnerability?” he said. Together, the photographer and his parents collected the artificial roses used in the photograph from wedding banquets they had recently attended, and Liu said the faux blooms represented some of the feelings he was grappling with. “I imagined myself as one of those plastic flowers: perhaps beautiful, but with no roots in the soil,” he described. “I could have a place at a wedding banquet, yet I felt unable to fulfill the traditional expectations of marriage, having children and carrying on the family line. For me, the flowers hold that tension I felt as a gay man facing my family’s expectations at the time.” Across “My Parents,” Liu explores ideas around companionship, intimacy, aging, gender expectations and cultural norms. In the beginning, Liu said each photograph could take months of discussion and conflict. For a long time, he didn’t know exactly why his father had agreed to take part in the work. His mother’s reasoning was more straightforward — she loved the besuited Taiwanese singer Fong Fei-fei and it was an opportunity to emulate her. But in 2014, when Liu invited his parents to speak alongside him during an artist talk, he was moved by his father’s words: He felt that wearing a wedding dress was a “low price” to pay to support his son, Liu recalled. “I do not assume that agreeing to be photographed means they accept all my ideas. But their willingness to make something with me means a great deal,” he said. Their differences have also influenced how he views art-making. “(My) participants have their own views of the work, which may differ from mine,” he said. “We can make a photograph together and gradually build understanding through that process.” Since he began making the work, life has changed for Taiwan’s LGBTQ community. Same-sex marriage was legalized in 2019, and the social climate, in turn, has become more accepting, though there are still generational differences, Liu said. Collaborating with his parents over such a long period has fundamentally changed their relationship as well. Today, Liu is married and all four of them live together (in Taiwan, like much of Asia, it is common for newlywed couples to live with one partner’s parents). He has begun traveling with his parents for the series as well, taking them to Thailand to celebrate Songkran, the water festival marking the New Year in the Theravada Buddhist calendar. Last year, they also joined him for two weeks during his artist residency in Kumamoto, Japan. He hopes that his work “encourages people to look again at images of family that have become so familiar that we no longer question them,” he said. As his parents age, he has thought more about care and the wellbeing of older LGBTQ people. “I hope discussions of gender equality can also address how we grow old, who cares for us, and whether we can live freely with the people we love,” he said. “To me, these are very tangible aspects of everyday life.”

images.caption: Liu's series on gender dynamics and cultural norms has also, over time, become a body of work about aging, intimacy and care.
Their collaborations didn't always come easy, but the artist is appreciative of the ways that all of their perspectives have shaped the work.

articles.title: Carlos Bardem lanza una petición para los españoles para las elecciones del 29N: "No volvamos a tiempos como en 'La Bola Negra'"
articles.standfirst: El actor avisa sobre el peligro de la censura y llama a la movilización masiva en las urnas
articles.summary: El actor avisa sobre el peligro de la censura y llama a la movilización masiva en las urnas
articles.body: El actor y escritor Carlos Bardem ha querido destacar el poder transformador de la cultura al señalar que 'La Bola Negra' es un perfecto ejemplo de cómo una película puede emocionar y, a partir de eso, generar cosas muy positivas. Durante su intervención, el intérprete puntualizó: "Esto que tú acabas de decir es muy importante", añadiendo en clave distendida que "yo aquí echo mi fichita de rojo profesional". Frente al panorama político actual, el artista advirtió con firmeza: "No volvamos a tiempos como esos, por favor". En esta línea, alertó de que "el 29 de noviembre nos jugamos volver a cosas como esa, nos jugamos a volver a la censura", y denunció una preocupante regresión cultural donde "ya están censurando películas, ya están censurando obras de teatro, ya están prohibiendo libros". Bardem profundizó en la defensa de los derechos individuales y civiles, exigiendo que "no volvamos a que una persona por amar a quien le salga del c*** o de donde le salga tenga que ocultarse, o tenga que pasar miedo, o sea agredida". Para el creador, la cita con las urnas es decisiva: "Nos jugamos cosas muy importantes el 29 de noviembre". Asimismo, quiso mandar un mensaje directo a las generaciones más jóvenes: "Yo animo a la gente joven, por favor, a los que piensan que las cosas no van con ellos y que, bueno, que da igual y que todos son iguales, no, no, todos no son todos iguales". Para combatir la desafección política, insistió en la necesidad de la acción ciudadana: "Y ir a votar". El intelectual reflexionó sobre cómo la ficción refleja peligros reales que creíamos superados: "Ir a votar porque eso que ves en la pantalla, en 'La Bola Negra' y que dices, 'Joder, ¿es posible que pasara esto?', bueno, pues eso pasaba, pasaba". Recordando que "eso está hace muy poquito", recalcó que "eso pasaba y esto hace muy poquito, y eso puede volver a pasar". Finalmente, el actor concluyó apelando a la responsabilidad colectiva y a la herramienta democrática fundamental: "Entonces está en nosotros que no pase". Por ello, zanjó recordando que "la herramienta que tenemos todos y todas es el voto".

articles.title: Salma Hayek says Halloween lets her play dress-up, but Dia de Muertos takes her back to her roots
articles.summary: Salma Hayek reflects on the significance of Halloween and Dia de Muertos, highlighting her Mexican heritage and the importance of remembering loved ones during the Day of the Dead celebrations.
articles.body: Hollywood actress Salma Hayek said that while Halloween lets her dress up and play a different character for the night, Dia de Muertos holds deeper emotional significance, bringing her back to her Mexican roots.Salma took to Instagram, where she shared a string of images from her Halloween celebrations, along with glimpses of how she marked Dia de Muertos. She said the occasion is about remembering loved ones who are no longer around by placing their photographs on altars and lighting candles in their memory.She wrote in the caption section: "After so many years of living between cultures, I've learned that I can embrace new traditions without letting go of the ones that shaped me.Halloween lets me play, dress up, and become someone else for a night this year, my beloved @penelopecruzoficial but Dia de Muertos always brings me back home. Today is not about costumes. It's about remembering."About placing a photo on the altar, lighting a candle, and making space for the people we still carry with us, even when they are no longer here. Two very different traditions, each with its own meaning, and both part of the life I've built between cultures. Happy Dia de los Muertos."Dia de los Muertos, or the Day of the Dead, is a multi-day holiday that involves family and friends gathering to pay respects and remember friends and family members who have died. articles.title: 'I am not The One': Suriya says 'The One' is not just his title but collective identity; recalls Nadippin Nayagan tag
articles.summary: The 'Scene' actor Suriya has explained why his latest title, 'The One', holds a special place in his heart.
articles.body: The 'Scene' actor Suriya has explained why his latest title, 'The One', holds a special place in his heart. During the audio launch of his upcoming Tamil film 'Scene', the actor said the name represents the collective bond he shares with his fans. He clarified that he does not consider it an individual identity or a personal tagline.Over the years, Suriya has been associated with several titles, including Nadippin Nayagan . However, he believes 'The One', which was entitled to him after the release of 'Retro', carries a different significance. According to the actor, the title reflects the unity between him and the people who have supported his journey. He also spoke about their unconditional affection and promised to continue entertaining them through his films. Suriya explains why 'The One' represents everyoneDuring his speech, Suriya explained that the title should not be understood as a name that sets him apart from his supporters. Instead, he considers it a representation of their collective identity."My connection with The One... I am not The One, it is The One because we are all one. We are one. In my mind, I don't see it as my name, my tagline. But I see it as... The One is all of us. Only with all of us it becomes The One," he said, as quoted by India Today.Actor describes his fans as one big familySuriya also spoke about the affection he has received from his supporters over the years. He described their connection as a family bond and said their love had remained unconditional. The actor acknowledged that a simple expression of gratitude would not be enough to recognise their continued support."So, for me, it is always that way. We are one, we are one family. This love is unconditional for so many years. One thank you will never do justice. I will always surrender (to you all), I will always be with you all, I will keep entertaining you on screen," he added.He assured the audience that he would continue to remain connected with them through his work.Suriya asks fans whether he should retain the titleThe actor also involved the audience in deciding whether 'The One' should continue to be part of his public identity. He sought their opinion about retaining the title during the audio launch.The moniker became associated with Suriya following his collaboration with filmmaker Karthik Subbaraj on 'Retro'. The audience responded positively when he brought up the subject, making their preference clear. Suriya acknowledged the enthusiastic reaction and agreed to continue using the title.'Scene' marks Suriya's third release of 2026Meanwhile, 'Scene' marks Suriya's third theatrical release of 2026, following 'Karuppu' and 'Vishwanath and Sons'. Written and directed by Jithu Madhavan, the upcoming Tamil action-comedy also stars Nazriya Nazim and Naslen.Suriya plays DSP Inbaraj, while Nazriya Nazim appears as Maya and Naslen portrays Eeswaran.
